comments.author: nik_s
comments.text:
I think the layman's perception of the increase in survival (~13 months versus ~6 months) will make this look underwhelming. Nevertheless, it's important to remember that the incentives for clinical trials is to only include very late-stage patients who have exhausted all other options (faster trials, smaller sample sizes, surrogate endpoints, a shot at accelerated approval, ...). The fact that a treatment shows promise for these patients that are often in very poor health and considered "hopeless" by today's medicine is exceedingly rare, and the signal from this trial is indeed strong.
The (somewhat reasonable) hope is that patients 1. with earlier forms of pancreatic cancer (non-metastatic) 2. that can undergo surgery 3. together with a (neo)adjuvant treatment with these kras inhibitors, will end up having a much lower recurrence rate and a chance for a long, healthy life.
I think this is genuinely good news worth celebrating!

I would recommend sticking to mainstream quantizations like the official GGML release, Unsloth's quants, or the more well known community quantizers like bartowski or AesSedai. comments.author: senko
comments.text:
This reminds me of a (completely different, but felt equally) bizzare problem with ghostty (the terminal emulator) on Linux and Steam, specifically Baldur's Gate 3.
At the start of the game after an update, BG3 compiles the (Vulkan) shaders. To avoid hammering the computer, it checks the load, including I/O pressure, and then throttles itself. It turns out that Ghostty uses io_uring, and even if it's not doing anything this somehow counts as pressure. This was made worse by the fact that I usually have a dozen or so Ghostty windows.
End result, BG3 compiles shaders using 1 core, throttled, instead of all available 20 cores. Instead of a minute or so, it'd take several hours.
(For closure: I configured ghostty to use epoll instead. Probably not optimal but works around the problem.)

Since lots of comments misunderstood the article, the extra latency from going through the monitor meant his laptop couldn't acknowledge the packets quickly enough. That led a buffer on the ethernet adapter to fill and that led it to drop packets.

It is quite a nice post which gets to the bottom of incredibly opaque behaviour of USB hubs.

comments.author: nagisa

I recently had this same problem with a multigig copper SFP+ module. These SFP+ modules (usually) advertise 10Gbps to the NIC they're plugged in, but will negotiate lower speeds on the copper side. So when NIC tries to send to SFP+ at higher rate than whatever speed SFP+ has negotiated internally, the SFP+ module will just drop a bunch of packets and incur a significant hit in throughput.
These tend to not support sending pause frames to its SFP+ side either, so the best option I found was to set bandwidth limit on the NIC…

The beta streaming tech is “pyrowave” and it is super low latency and looks INCREDIBLE compared to traditional codecs, but as a trade off it is extremely sensitive to packet loss, and uses an appropriately large amount of bandwidth (7-800mbit at 4k120). Wired network isn’t _strictly_ a requirement but it might as well be, and the steam deck doesn’t have a physical port - but the steam deck dock does.
Anyway, the exact same situation arises, where some network condition or physical configuration (there’s a lot of hardware in between these two devices, including MoCA adapters) meant that the network adapter buffer fills up and starts dropping packets. The buffer size is configurable through some terminal command and maxing that out makes the issue disappear immediately.

C# already provides many tools for your performance-critical code though. You can use pointers in unsafe. You can allocate unmanaged memory with Marshal. You can avoid copy with Span. You can even manually vectorise with Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated and such.

I'm sure there are people who want a C# without GC, but for me it's just... sufficient enough.

comments.author: bob1029
comments.text:
The GC is a feature. Not a bug to be eliminated.
GC is not surrendering control. That seems to be HN's #1 bug bear. The sensation that someone or something is taking control away from you. The proper way to frame this is that you can actually focus on the original problem you set out to solve. Risking memory leaks is crazy when it's not something the customer is demanding. Even in gaming I think the GC is fine. There are ways to spread the impact across frames and bound the amount of time spent collecting.
If your clever scheme wouldn't work with a GC-managed heap, it probably won't work with one managed by hand either.

comments.author: YuechenLi

So... What does this have over using NativeAOT which already exists?
Keep in mind a large portion of time NativeAOT is actually SLOWER than going through RyuJIT with the only definitive benefit being smaller binaries, and it's not like you can't do Span<T> and ref structs in modern C# for manual low level memory control already.
So my question is just... why?

comments.author: andix
comments.text:
Assuming this is very similar to bflat: it's a cool idea and fun to play with, but not very useful. C# is not designed to run without a GC, existing code usually won't run, because the standard library is missing.
Just using C, Rust, Zig, or whatever is probably nearly always the better option. Those languages are designed to work without GC and provide various well established ways to manage memory.

comments.author: buybackoff
comments.text:
For C# as is, what I really would appreciate is a frozen GC mode. Not zero GC, similar to Epsilon GC in Java. After initial state loading and forced GC, I would like to be able to apply a SustainedNoGC mode, that just does not even try to collect, no scanning, no pauses at all, it can only allocate. And notifications (an event) after some X bytes allocated, or just a reliable way to monitor the allocated size. The existing modes such as SustainedLowLatency or NoGCRegion are good but not enough. For some low latency workloads it's OK to allocate many GBs and then pause explicitly.
Random forced pauses are the only problem that comes from GC, otherwise it's great for throughput and just a nice feature, as a sibling comment says. No GC languages do not make code magically faster, they still have malloc/free. However, GC is surrendering control over when a program may be paused.

comments.author: showcaseearth
comments.text:
Lovely work!! On “Where did you paint this?”, I've gotten this myself as I've painted off and on over the years too, mostly landscapes. It's what drove me to start a side project years ago to put art on the map (consolidate specific viewpoints, photo comparisons, streetview, historic maps, etc). As those things go, I never got beyond a crude app while life competed for resources. Picked it back up this year, hoping to "launch" a first version soon. Mostly historical stuff because that's what's openly available, but maybe someday it could be a tool for placing my own and other artists' contemporary work!
I approached the same “static for everyone, dynamic for me” need from a different angle. Instead of building my own editor, I use self hosted Grist instance with customized widgets. Publishing means building a versioned snapshot of the catalog and pointing a tiny current.json at it. Old versions never change, so they cache forever and nothing needs invalidating. Staging and production are just two pointers, and rolling back means pointing back at the previous version.

stories.title_en: We promoted developers into architects without informing them

comments.author: whycombinetor
comments.text:
Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed? Even when the org was large to have an architect, they just were just a figurehead and designed the original system, and ongoing decisions were made by the dev who picks up the ticket.
From that perspective, engineers are still engineers, just without the hands-on-keyboard coding. If that's all your job was, hands-on-keyboard coding with no decision making, yeah you're cooked and need to reskill.

comments.author: nixpulvis
comments.text:
I strongly believe good software teams (very rare) require members to play many roles. Sometimes you're a PM, sometimes you're an architect, sometimes you're the systems engineer. Enough people have enough context on the bigger picture that it's stable and there's a shared vision.
More often than not, one person does the majority of this, and does their best to break up the responsibilities. A good CTO does that at the top, and it flows down through the ranks depending on how big the org is. Perhaps it's just a CTO and 5 engineers, perhaps it's a CTO with 5 divisions, each with 10 groups, with many teams.
Flatter structures of engaged members works best from what I've seen, but you need to have a critical mass of people not only willing to take initiative, but empowered by leadership.
